subject: Meteorology
learning_objective: Apply the ISA temperature lapse rate
question_text: In the ISA, what is the approximate temperature at 5,000 ft?
explanation: The ISA lapse rate is 1.98 degrees C per 1,000 ft (6.5 degrees C per km). 15 - (5 x 1.98) = 5.1, about +5 degrees C.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That uses a lapse rate of only 1 degree C per 1,000 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That uses a lapse rate of 4 degrees C per 1,000 ft.

calculation_steps: T = 15 - 1.98 x 5 = 15 - 9.9 = 5.1 deg C, approximately +5 deg C

subject: Meteorology
learning_objective: Explain altimeter error when flying towards lower pressure
question_text: An aeroplane flies from an area of high pressure towards an area of low pressure without the altimeter subscale being reset. How does the true altitude compare with the indicated altitude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The aeroplane is higher than indicated

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aeroplane is at the indicated altitude

choices.label: C
choices.text: The aeroplane is lower than indicated

choices.label: D
choices.text: It depends only on the outside air temperature

explanation: Holding a constant indicated altitude means following a constant-pressure surface. That surface slopes down towards low pressure, so the aeroplane descends while the altimeter shows no change. Hence the saying 'from high to low, look out below'.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That happens when flying from low towards high pressure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Unless the subscale is reset, the altimeter does not compensate for the pressure change.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Temperature also matters, but the pressure change alone makes the altimeter over-read here.

question_text: With QNH set on the subscale, what does an altimeter read when the aeroplane is on the ground at the aerodrome?

subject: Meteorology
question_text: An aerodrome is at 500 ft elevation and the QNH is 1003 hPa. Assuming 30 ft per hPa, what does the altimeter read on the ground with 1013 hPa set?
explanation: Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 - QNH) x 30 ft = 500 + 10 x 30 = 800 ft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The correction has been applied in the wrong direction; with QNH below 1013, pressure altitude is higher than elevation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That is the reading with QNH set.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The pressure difference is 10 hPa (300 ft), not about 27 hPa.

question_text: What is the dew point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The temperature at which water freezes in the air

choices.label: B
choices.text: The temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure, to become saturated

choices.label: C
choices.text: The temperature difference between the air and the ground

choices.label: D
choices.text: The temperature at which relative humidity is 50 percent

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Dew point is a property of the air's moisture content.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: At the dew point the relative humidity is 100 percent.

subject: Meteorology
question_text: Which combination of conditions most favours radiation fog?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An overcast night with strong wind over the sea

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sunny afternoon with low humidity

choices.label: C
choices.text: A clear night, light wind and moist air over land

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warm moist air moving over a cold sea surface

explanation: Clear skies let the ground radiate heat away overnight. Light wind (a few knots) cools a shallow layer of moist air to its dew point without dispersing it. This happens over land, because the sea's temperature changes little overnight.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cloud cover stops radiative cooling and strong wind mixes the air.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Radiation fog forms when the ground cools at night.

question_text: How does advection fog form?

choices.text: The ground cools by radiation on a clear, calm night

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cold air moves over warmer water and steam rises

subject: Meteorology
learning_objective: Identify the stages of a thunderstorm
question_text: Which stage of a thunderstorm is marked by both strong updraughts and downdraughts, and by precipitation reaching the ground?
explanation: A thunderstorm cell has a cumulus stage (updraughts), a mature stage (updraughts and downdraughts, heavy precipitation, gust front, the worst turbulence, hail and lightning) and a dissipating stage (downdraughts).

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The developing stage is dominated by updraughts; precipitation has not yet reached the ground.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The dissipating stage is dominated by downdraughts.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The anvil is a feature of the mature cell, not a separate stage.

subject: Meteorology
question_text: In the northern hemisphere, a pilot stands with their back to the wind. Where is the area of low pressure?
explanation: Buys Ballot's law: in the northern hemisphere, with your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left. Coriolis deflection makes air circulate anticlockwise around a low.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: That applies in the southern hemisphere.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Above the friction layer the wind blows roughly parallel to the isobars, not straight into low pressure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Air flows from high towards low pressure, not the other way.

subject: Meteorology
learning_objective: Explain the effect of surface friction on wind
question_text: In the northern hemisphere, compared with the wind at 2,000 ft, how is the surface wind usually different?
explanation: Friction slows the surface wind. A slower wind feels less Coriolis force, so the pressure gradient turns it towards low pressure. In the northern hemisphere that is a backing (anticlockwise) shift, typically about 30 degrees over land.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Friction slows the surface wind, and the reduced Coriolis effect backs it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Over the northern hemisphere the surface wind backs relative to the gradient wind.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Surface friction changes both speed and direction.

subject: Meteorology
learning_objective: Determine the ceiling from a METAR
question_text: A METAR reports FEW012 SCT030 BKN080. What is the ceiling?
explanation: The ceiling is the height of the base of the lowest cloud layer covering more than half the sky (BKN or OVC) below 20,000 ft (6,000 m). Here that is BKN at 080, i.e. 8,000 ft.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: FEW (1-2 oktas) does not form a ceiling.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: SCT (3-4 oktas) does not form a ceiling.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: BKN (5-7 oktas) covers more than half the sky and forms a ceiling.

question_text: Which weather is typical of an unstable air mass?

choices.text: Stratiform cloud, drizzle and poor visibility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear skies, fog and smooth air

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cumuliform cloud, showers, turbulence and good visibility outside the showers

choices.label: D

subject: Meteorology
question_text: Moist air is forced over a mountain range, producing cloud and precipitation on the windward side. What is typical on the lee side?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Warmer and drier air at the same level (foehn)

explanation: On the windward side, air cools at the slower saturated rate once cloud forms and loses water as precipitation. Descending on the lee side, it warms at the faster dry rate, so it arrives warmer and drier than it started.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Air descending on the lee side warms at the dry adiabatic rate.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Losing moisture as precipitation makes the descending air warmer and drier.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The lee side typically has warm, dry, clearer air.
